about: Spans the Phase 14 journeys need: the British Empire (Empires journey), Greek philosophy and Mahavira (Ideas journey).

spans.name: British Empire
spans.date_display: 1607 (Jamestown, the first lasting colony) to 1997 (the handover of Hong Kong); some date it from Newfoundland, 1583
spans.description: The colonies, trading posts, protectorates and dominions ruled by England and then Britain, built by settlement, trade and conquest. At its height it covered about a quarter of the world's land and people; most of it became independent in the decades after the Second World War.
spans.significance: It spread the English language, common law, parliamentary government and sports such as cricket around the world, and its trade and investment tied distant economies together. It also rested on conquest and, until abolition, on slavery: British ships were the leading carriers of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic in the 1700s. Its legacy is still argued over in Britain and in its former colonies.
spans.note: There is no single founding date. 1607 (Jamestown) is the first permanent settlement; Gilbert claimed Newfoundland in 1583. 1997 (Hong Kong) is the usual end.

spans.name: Greek Philosophy from Thales to Aristotle
spans.date_display: c. 585 BCE (Thales) to 322 BCE (the death of Aristotle)
spans.description: The Greek thinkers who tried to explain the world by observation, reason and argument rather than myth: the natural philosophers of Ionia, then Socrates, Plato and Aristotle in Athens. After Aristotle, new schools such as the Stoics and Epicureans carried Greek philosophy on for centuries.
spans.significance: Their habits of definition, logical argument and testing ideas against evidence became the foundation of Western philosophy and science. Scholars writing in Arabic, and later in Latin, translated and debated Plato and Aristotle for nearly two thousand years.
spans.note: The start is conventional: Thales is traditionally the first Greek philosopher, and his eclipse prediction (585 BCE, reported by Herodotus) is the usual marker. Ancient Greek philosophy as a whole runs on to late antiquity; this span covers its founding era only, hence the name.

spans.name: Life of Mahavira
spans.date_display: traditionally 599–527 BCE; many historians place him later, as an older contemporary of the Buddha
spans.description: Vardhamana, called Mahavira ('great hero'), revered by Jains as the 24th and last tirthankara, or teacher who shows the way to liberation. In the Ganges valley he taught non-violence toward all living beings, truthfulness and strict self-discipline.
spans.significance: Jainism's ideal of non-violence (ahimsa) toward every living thing shaped Indian ethics, vegetarianism and trade communities. It also influenced Gandhi, whose early mentor Shrimad Rajchandra was a Jain thinker.
spans.note: Dates follow the Svetambara tradition (Digambaras give 615 BCE for his birth), the same approach as the Buddha's span.

links.why: The return of Hong Kong to China is usually taken as the end of the British Empire.
Crown rule in India was the largest part of the British Empire.
The East India Company ruled under a royal charter, so historians count its Indian territories in the empire, though the Crown took direct control only in 1858.
Thales is traditionally the first Greek philosopher, and his eclipse prediction is the usual marker of the start.
Plato's Academy in Athens was the era's leading school; Aristotle studied there for twenty years.
Socrates's trial and death, recorded by his pupil Plato, are a central episode of Greek philosophy.
Jaspers counted the Greek philosophers among the Axial Age's thinkers; historians debate the label.
Mahavira taught in the same centuries and region as the Buddha; historians debate the Axial Age label.
